Mercy is portrayed as a higher, more benevolent force than the rigid demands of justice.  
Portia explains that “the quality of mercy … droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven” and that it “blesseth him that gives and him that takes.” She contrasts this with the “mightiest in the mightiest,” describing how a monarch’s sceptre represents temporal power, yet “mercy is above this sceptred sway; It is enthroned in the hearts of kings.” Thus mercy is seen as an attribute of God and a superior virtue to mere legal or political authority.  

In contrast, Shylock’s speech focuses on the strict application of law: he demands that “the penalty and forfeit of my bond” be carried out, emphasizing the procedural justice owed to him rather than any merciful consideration. This underscores how mercy is viewed as a deliberate choice beyond the automatic enforcement of legal penalties.

- Portia’s description of mercy versus power: “The quality of mercy … droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven… It is enthroned in the hearts of kings…”  
- Shylock’s insistence on legal penalty: “My deeds upon my head! I crave the law, The penalty and forfeit of my bond.”
